claims.text: Acute self-limited diarrhea: usually no tests.
claims.quote: Testing is unnecessary in most cases of acute self-limited diarrhea.

claims.text: Directed testing when the picture points away from viral gastroenteritis.
claims.quote: However, if the evaluation suggests an etiology other than viral gastroenteritis, testing should be directed by the suspected etiology

claims.text: Suspected bacterial diarrhea (fever, bloody stool, abdominal pain): stool culture and fecal leukocytes.
claims.quote: Fever, bloody stool, abdominal pain Possibly petechiae or pallor (in patients with hemolytic uremic syndrome) History of contact with animals ( E. coli ) or reptiles ( Salmonella ) History of eating undercooked food ( Salmonella ) Recent ( < 2 months) antibiotic use ( C. difficile ) Day care center outbreak Stool culture Fecal leukocytes
claims.locator: Table: Some Causes of Diarrhea in Children (Bacteria)

claims.text: Ill-appearing child: CBC, renal function tests and blood culture.
claims.quote: If patients appear ill, complete blood count, renal function tests, and blood culture
claims.locator: Table: Some Causes of Diarrhea in Children

claims.text: Recent antibiotics: stool test for C. difficile toxin.
claims.quote: If patient has recently been given antibiotics, stool testing for C. difficile toxin
claims.locator: Table: Some Causes of Diarrhea in Children

claims.text: Suspected parasites: stool microscopy for ova and parasites, and stool antigen or PCR tests.
claims.quote: Microscopic examination of stool for ova and parasites Stool antigen or PCR tests
claims.locator: Table: Some Causes of Diarrhea in Children (Parasites)

claims.text: Celiac disease: tissue transglutaminase (tTG) and endomysial (EMA) antibodies, sometimes small-bowel biopsy.
claims.quote: Testing may include the serologic marker anti-tissue transglutaminase antibody (tTG) and the anti-endomysial antibody (EMA) and sometimes small-bowel biopsy.
